subject: Access pattern recommendation for Atlas Health private deployment
messages:
From: Alice Thomas <alice.thomas@atlashealth.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: devops@atlashealth.com
Date: Thu, 22 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Architect question — connectivity for private deploy

Hi Ben,

We’re moving ahead with Redwood Private inside our AWS account and the security team asked us to pick a single recommended network access pattern: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or site-to-site VPN.

High level constraints: we must keep egress tightly controlled, minimize blast radius (least privileged access), and avoid complex NATs for cross-account traffic. Latency requirements are moderate (95th percentile token latency ~150ms). Cost matters but is secondary to security.

Attached is a simple network snapshot of our VPCs. Can you advise which path you recommend and any gotchas we should flag to our infra team?

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick call if helpful.

— Alice
Director, Cloud Platform
Atlas Health

Attachments: atlas_network_snapshot.png

Subject: Re: Architect question — connectivity for private deploy

Hi Alice — thanks for the diagram and the clarity on constraints. I looped in Karthik (solutions architect) and Marissa (customer success) to make sure we cover security and operational tradeoffs. Quick summary up-front: PrivateLink is usually the safest across account boundaries (least privileged, no route table changes), peering can be simpler for high-throughput internal traffic but increases attack surface if misconfigured, and S2S VPN is the lowest-friction but has the weakest isolation and higher management overhead.

Karthik — could you do a short pros/cons list tailored to Atlas’s snapshot and call out things like cross-account security controls, egress, and how our connector (Redwood Private agent) behaves in each mode? We’ve also attached a one-page PrivateLink cheatsheet that helps explain port-level requirements.

Ben
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>, Alice Thomas <alice.thomas@atlashealth.com>
Date: Thu, 22 Apr 2027 13:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Architect question — connectivity for private deploy

Thanks — digging into specifics for Atlas Health and the attached VPC diagram. Below are concise, actionable pros/cons plus implementation notes for each pattern.

1) PrivateLink (AWS Interface Endpoints) — recommended baseline for Atlas
- Pros:
  - Strong isolation: host-level endpoint services expose only the required ports; customers keep control of route tables and security groups.
  - Least privilege: we present an endpoint service; Atlas accepts the endpoint into their VPC, no peering routes are added.
  - Works well across accounts and regions with ALB/NLB fronting if needed.
- Cons / Gotchas:
  - Slightly higher per-GB dataplane cost than peering.
  - Requires careful SG rules; misses out on path-level visibility unless you add VPC Flow Logs or a Transit Gateway.
- Redwood-specific notes:
  - Our private connector supports being behind an interface endpoint. You must allow outbound TLS (443) from the connector subnets to the endpoint ENIs.
  - If you need customer-initiated callbacks into Atlas resources, we recommend a narrow set of endpoints rather than broad network access.

2) VPC Peering — good for high-throughput but with caveats
- Pros:
  - Low-latency, no per-GB interface endpoint charges.
  - Transparent network routing; easier if you need internal-only traffic and many services talk to each other.
- Cons / Gotchas:
  - Peering is transitive-unaware; managing multiple peers at scale becomes a routing headache.
  - Risk: accidental routing exposure can increase blast radius if route tables expand.
  - Cross-account IAM/flow controls are weaker; you must rely on SGs/NACLs to mitigate.
- Redwood-specific notes:
  - For peering, we surface an allowlist of CIDR ranges the Redwood nodes will use; ensure no overlap with Atlas CIDRs.
  - If Atlas expects to route to other internal subnets, consider Transit Gateway instead of many peering links.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPSec) — quick to stand up, heavier ops
- Pros:
  - Fast proof-of-concept; often used when customers cannot accept endpoint services.
  - Can be encrypted over public internet without account-level changes.
- Cons / Gotchas:
  - Bandwidth and latency variability; keep this for low-throughput or admin/control plane traffic.
  - Key rotation and tunnel health need monitoring; adds operational load to Atlas.
- Redwood-specific notes:
  - We can route control plane traffic over a VPN but recommend using VPN only as fallback or for restricted maintenance windows.

Recommendation for Atlas Health (given security-first constraint):
- Primary: PrivateLink for normal inference traffic (least privileged by default).
- If low-latency bulk transfer is required for model prefetch or large batch jobs, consider a dedicated peering link or Transit Gateway adjacency for that limited subnet.
- VPN: keep as emergency/failover connectivity with strict ACLs and monitoring.

Next steps:
- Marissa, I’d suggest we produce a short mutual action plan that lists required Atlas tasks (approve endpoint service, create SGs, identify connector subnets) and Redwood tasks (provide endpoint service name, sample SG rules, test plan). Ben — once Alice confirms, we’ll schedule a 30-minute technical sync.

— Karthik
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Thanks Karthik — that is very helpful and aligns with what our security folks were leaning toward. Two quick clarifications:
1) For PrivateLink, will we need to open more than 443 from connector subnets?
2) If we accept the endpoint, will Redwood ever initiate connections into our VPC beyond that endpoint SG/ports?

If you can confirm those two, we’ll mark PrivateLink as preferred and I’ll route the mutual action plan to our infra team.

— Alice

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Alice Thomas <alice.thomas@atlashealth.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com, neha_kapoor@redwood.com
Date: Thu, 22 Apr 2027 15:46:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Architect question — connectivity for private deploy (next steps)

Alice — answers below and a short next-step list.

1) PrivateLink port requirements: no, in 99% of cases you only need outbound TLS (443) from the connector subnets to the interface endpoint ENIs. If you plan to use non-HTTP transports for internal callbacks, we’ll call that out explicitly in the mutual action plan.

2) Redwood traffic into your VPC: we will not initiate arbitrary connections into your VPC. Traffic terminates at the endpoint service; any additional access requires explicit configuration and is always documented in the MAP.

Next steps (proposed):
- Ben: send MAP draft (attached) and HubSpot update (DL-1342).
- Alice: confirm endpoint acceptance and identify the connector subnets to expose to the endpoint.
- Karhthik/Neha: schedule 30-minute technical sync once Atlas confirms (calendar invite pending).

I attached a starter mutual action plan and the PrivateLink cheatsheet for your infra team. Let me know times that work for the sync.

Best,
Ben
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
